all_historical_figures.name: Aśoka
all_historical_figures.significance: Patronized Buddhist, Jaina, and Ājīvika sects, showing broad religious support.
all_historical_figures.dates: c. 268 to 232 BCE (not specified in text)

all_historical_figures.name: Kaniṣka
all_historical_figures.significance: Patronized all religious sects, including folk cults.
all_historical_figures.dates: c. 127 to 150 AD (not specified in text)

all_historical_figures.name: Harṣa-vardhana
all_historical_figures.significance: Patronized all religious sects, including folk cults.
all_historical_figures.dates: c. 606 to 647 AD (not specified in text)

all_historical_figures.name: Sātāvahana kings
all_historical_figures.significance: Identified as Śaivas, but built many Buddhist shrines.

all_historical_figures.name: Kākutstha-Varma
all_historical_figures.significance: Follower of Vedic religion who gave land grants to a Jaina ascetic.

all_historical_figures.name: Śruta-kīrti
all_historical_figures.significance: Recipient of a land grant from Kākutstha-Varma.

all_historical_figures.name: Mṛgeśa-varma
all_historical_figures.significance: Gave grants for Jaina shrines.

all_historical_figures.name: Ravi-varma
all_historical_figures.significance: Built a Jinālaya (Jain temple).

all_historical_figures.name: Maṅgalīśa
all_historical_figures.significance: A devotee of Śiva who excavated a famous rock-cut shrine for Viṣṇu.

all_historical_figures.name: Kṛtti-varma I
all_historical_figures.significance: Predecessor and elder brother of Maṅgalīśa; a devotee of Viṣṇu who conceived the Viṣṇu shrine.

all_historical_figures.name: Biṭṭiga-Viṣṇuvardhana
all_historical_figures.significance: Built the Keśava temple at Belūr but was personally a Jaina.

all_historical_figures.name: Rāmānuja
all_historical_figures.significance: Mentioned in the context of the (disputed) story of Viṣṇuvardhana's conversion.

all_historical_figures.name: Vikramāditya VI
all_historical_figures.significance: A devotee of Śiva who endowed a Buddhist vihāra and built a Śiva temple with sculptures of Viṣṇu.

all_historical_figures.name: Kṛṣṇadeva-rāya
all_historical_figures.significance: A Vaiṣṇava who made rich endowments to Śiva temples.

all_historical_figures.name: Kokkalla-māharāja
all_historical_figures.significance: His praśasti (eulogy inscription) begins with a prayer to an all-comprehensive God.

all_historical_figures.name: Jayasimha
all_historical_figures.significance: His inscription of 1022 refers to a 'traipuruṣa' temple built by Akkadevī.

all_historical_figures.name: Akkadevī
all_historical_figures.significance: Built a temple for Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva, while practicing rituals of Jina, Buddha, Viṣṇu, and Śiva.

all_historical_figures.name: Nāga-varma
all_historical_figures.significance: Built four shrines for Jina, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and Buddha.

all_historical_figures.name: Siddhi-nṛsiṁha-malla
all_historical_figures.significance: His 'praśasti' contains a verse adoring the trinity.

all_historical_figures.name: Harihara-siṁha
all_historical_figures.significance: Father of Siddhi-nṛsiṁha-malla.

all_historical_figures.name: Vijayāditya
all_historical_figures.significance: Built the Vijayeśvara ('trai-puruśa') temple in Bādāmi in memory of his mother.

all_historical_figures.name: Vinayavatī
all_historical_figures.significance: Mother of Vijayāditya, in whose memory the Vijayeśvara temple was built.

all_historical_figures.name: Vijaya-sena
all_historical_figures.significance: Built the 'advaita-līlāgṛha' temple for Pradyumneśvara (joint Śiva-Viṣṇu).

all_historical_figures.name: Polāļva
all_historical_figures.role: Minister of Hoysala king Narasimha II
all_historical_figures.significance: Built a separate shrine for the composite deity Hari-Hara.

all_historical_figures.name: Narasimha II
all_historical_figures.significance: King under whom the minister Polāļva served.

all_historical_figures.name: Nāganikā
all_historical_figures.significance: Her Nānāghāṭ inscription mentions only male deities.

all_historical_figures.name: Sātakarni II
all_historical_figures.significance: Husband of queen Nāganikā.

all_historical_figures.name: Hāla
all_historical_figures.significance: Author of Gāthā-saptaśatī which invokes Śiva as husband of Gauri.

all_historical_figures.name: Pāṇini
all_historical_figures.significance: His work shows acquaintance with Śiva's names (Mṛḍā, Bhava, Sarva), indicating the god's worship in his time.

all_historical_figures.name: Aśoka
all_historical_figures.significance: According to Kalhaṇa's Rājataranginī, he visited Kāśhmir and erected a shrine to Śiva called Aśokeśvara.

all_historical_figures.name: Kalhaṇa
all_historical_figures.significance: His work, Rājataranginī, is cited as the source for Aśoka's connection to Śaivism in Kashmir.

all_historical_figures.name: Kautilya
all_historical_figures.significance: Prescribed that a temple to Śiva must be erected within the city.

all_historical_figures.name: Patañjali
all_historical_figures.significance: Made explicit reference to 'Śiva-bhāgavatas' (devotees of Śiva) and the selling of Śiva icons by the Mauryas.

all_historical_figures.name: John Marśal
all_historical_figures.significance: Found a 1st century B.C. bronze seal at Sirkāp (Taxila) with an iconic representation of Śiva.

all_historical_figures.name: Vainya-gupta
all_historical_figures.significance: Recorded as being a 'great devotee of Śiva', indicating the religion's crystallization by the Gupta era.

all_historical_figures.name: Mihira-gula
all_historical_figures.significance: Was a worshipper of Śiva as Paśupati; his coins featured Śiva's bull insignia.

all_historical_figures.name: Śrīkaṇṭha
all_historical_figures.significance: Believed in some traditions to have received the Śaiva teachings directly from Śiva and transmitted them to disciples. Appears to have been a historical figure.

all_historical_figures.name: Bhairava
all_historical_figures.significance: Received the Śaiva teachings from Śrīkaṇṭha.

all_historical_figures.name: Durvāsas
all_historical_figures.significance: In Kāśmir Śaivism, believed to have received the āgamas from Śiva (as Śrīkaṇṭha) and taught different philosophical paths to his disciples.

all_historical_figures.name: Tryambaka, Āmardaka and Śrīkaṇṭha
all_historical_figures.significance: Taught the philosophies of non-dualism (abheda), dualism (bheda), and dualism-and-non-dualism (bhedābheda) respectively.

all_historical_figures.name: Lakulīśa
all_historical_figures.significance: A key historical figure who systematized and propagated Pāśupata Śaivism. Hailed as an incarnation of Śiva.

all_historical_figures.name: Kuśika, Gārgya, Maitreya, Karūśa
all_historical_figures.significance: Four highly regarded disciples who started their own lines of teaching (catuśśākhā).

all_historical_figures.name: Kauśika
all_historical_figures.significance: Probable author of the Pāśupata-sūtra, the definitive text of the system.

all_historical_figures.name: Kauṇḍinya (Rāśi-kara)
all_historical_figures.significance: Prepared the Pañcārtha-Bhāṣya, a commentary on the Pāśupata-sūtra.

all_historical_figures.name: Bhāsarvajña
all_historical_figures.significance: Wrote the Ratna-ṭīkā, a gloss on Haradatta's Gaṇa-kārikā, linking the Pāśupata system to Āgama literature.

all_historical_figures.name: Haradatta
all_historical_figures.significance: Wrote the Gaṇa-kārikā.

all_historical_figures.name: Bhujaṅga-Deva
all_historical_figures.significance: Founded the 'Bhujaṅgāvali' lineage of the Kālāmukha sect.

all_historical_figures.name: Sureśvara-paṇḍita-deva
all_historical_figures.significance: Mentioned in a 1057 A.D. inscription, linking the Kālāmukha sect to Lākula's doctrines and the Śrīśaila center.

all_historical_figures.name: Kṛṣṇa III
all_historical_figures.significance: His Karhaḍ inscription records a land grant to a Śaiva ascetic, showing royal patronage.

all_historical_figures.name: Gaṅga-śiva
all_historical_figures.significance: Recipient of a land grant from Kṛṣṇa III, described as a leader in the Śaiva sect.

all_historical_figures.name: Īśāna-śiva
all_historical_figures.significance: Preceptor of Gaṅga-śiva.

all_historical_figures.name: Kīrtivarman
all_historical_figures.significance: Constructed a pavilion in the Nīlakaṇṭha temple at the instance of his Pāśupata preceptor.

all_historical_figures.name: Śrī-mūrti
all_historical_figures.significance: Preceptor of King Kīrtivarman.

all_historical_figures.name: Durlabhā-devī
all_historical_figures.significance: Made land grants to the Mahākuṭa temple.

all_historical_figures.name: Maṅgalīśa
all_historical_figures.significance: His inscription mentions the land grants of Durlabhā-devī, confirming early Śaiva activity in Karnataka.

all_historical_figures.name: Kālaśakti
all_historical_figures.significance: Mentioned in a 640 A.D. inscription at Nandi, indicating an early Kālāmukha center.

all_historical_figures.name: Ratnāvaḷī
all_historical_figures.significance: Made a grant to Kālaśakti's disciple, showing patronage.

all_historical_figures.name: Īśvaradeva
all_historical_figures.significance: Recipient of a grant from Ratnāvaḷī.

all_historical_figures.name: Mahendra
all_historical_figures.significance: A great warrior king and 'parama-māheśvara' who dedicated his palace to Śiva.

all_historical_figures.name: Ananta-śiva-deva
all_historical_figures.significance: Presided over the large university attached to the Noḷambeśvara temple at Heñjeru.

all_historical_figures.name: Kedāra-śakti
all_historical_figures.significance: Founded the Kedāreśvara temple and Kōḍiya-maṭha at Balligāme.

all_historical_figures.name: Someśvara II ('Bhuvanaika-malla')
all_historical_figures.significance: A zealous Śaiva who patronized Kālāmukha shrines.

all_historical_figures.name: Pērmāḍi-Vikramāditya VI ('Tribhuvana-malla')
all_historical_figures.significance: Although a Jaina, he extended patronage to Kālāmukha shrines. The dates 1706-1127 are a clear typographical error in the source text; the correct reign is 1076-1127.

all_historical_figures.name: Someśvara
all_historical_figures.significance: Administered the Nagareśvara temple at Sūḍi and was praised in an inscription for his broad learning and tolerance.

all_historical_figures.name: Bijjaḷa II
all_historical_figures.significance: His minister, Keśirāja, was a patron of the Kālāmukha sect. He was also the king whom Basava served.

all_historical_figures.name: Keśirāja-daṇḍādhīśa (Keśimayya)
all_historical_figures.significance: Follower of the Kālāmukha master Vāmaśakti-dēva, built a temple to Keśava.

all_historical_figures.name: Vāmaśakti-dēva
all_historical_figures.significance: Was the revered preceptor ('ārādhya') of minister Keśirāja.

all_historical_figures.name: Trilocana-munīndra
all_historical_figures.significance: Mentioned in an inscription as making a land donation to a dancing girl, suggesting Kālāmukha involvement with the devadāsī system.

all_historical_figures.name: Nāgadevayya
all_historical_figures.significance: Built the Nāgeśvara temple at Sūndi and a township for temple prostitutes.

all_historical_figures.name: Harihara I
all_historical_figures.significance: His Rājaguru was the Kālāmukha teacher Kāśivilāsa-kriyāśakti.

all_historical_figures.name: Bukka
all_historical_figures.significance: His Rājaguru was the Kālāmukha teacher Kāśivilāsa-kriyāśakti.

all_historical_figures.name: Kāśivilāsa-kriyāśakti
all_historical_figures.significance: Was the Rājaguru of Harihara I and Bukka, administered the Virūpākṣa temple at Hampi, and was honored by the Vidyāśaṅkara shrine at Śṛṅgeri.

all_historical_figures.name: Basava
all_historical_figures.significance: Spearheaded the Vīraśaiva movement, which led to the decline of the Kālāmukhas and their absorption into the new creed.

all_historical_figures.name: Haradatta
all_historical_figures.significance: Author of Gaņa-kārikā, which points to the Pāśupata sect's reliance on Śaivāgamas.

all_historical_figures.name: Abhinava-gupta
all_historical_figures.significance: A major exponent of Kāśmir Śaivism and the Pratyabhijñā school. Authored key texts like Tantrāloka and Pratyabhijñā-vimarśinī. Argued for a non-dualistic interpretation of the Āgamas.
all_historical_figures.dates: towards the close of the tenth century A.D.

all_historical_figures.name: Vasugupta
all_historical_figures.significance: Popularized the non-dualistic Śiva-sūtra, which he is said to have discovered, laying the groundwork for Kāśmīr Śaivism.

all_historical_figures.name: Kallaṭa
all_historical_figures.significance: Propagated Vasugupta's teachings, specifically the Spanda' kārikā, and authored Spanda-Sarvasva, contributing to the Spanda-śāstra division.

all_historical_figures.name: Somānanda
all_historical_figures.significance: Authored Śiva-dṛṣṭi, the definitive text of the Pratyabhijñā school, and is hailed as the 'maker of logic' (tarkasya kartā).

all_historical_figures.name: Utpala
all_historical_figures.significance: Wrote the Kārikās on Pratyabhijñā, which helped crystallize the school's fundamental concepts.

all_historical_figures.name: Lakṣaṇa-gupta
all_historical_figures.significance: Was the student of Utpala and the teacher of the great Abhinava-gupta.

all_historical_figures.name: Śambhu-nātha
all_historical_figures.significance: A master from Jālandhara who initiated Abhinava-gupta into Āgama wisdom.

all_historical_figures.name: Sadyojyoti
all_historical_figures.significance: Credited with first using the term 'Siddhānta' for the Āgamic tradition and revealing the 'royal road' to Śiva-siddhānta. Hailed as the 'kulaguru' of the school.

all_historical_figures.name: Bṛhaspati
all_historical_figures.significance: Colleague of Sadyojyoti, also credited with establishing the Siddhānta school.

all_historical_figures.name: Ugra-jyoti
all_historical_figures.significance: Teacher of Sadyojyoti.

all_historical_figures.name: Rājānaka-Rāmakaṇṭha
all_historical_figures.significance: A scholar from Kāśmīra who wrote a commentary on Sadyojyoti's Mokṣa-kārikā.

all_historical_figures.name: Jayaratha
all_historical_figures.significance: Commentator on Abhinava-gupta's work.

all_historical_figures.name: Aghora-śiva
all_historical_figures.significance: Valiantly defended the dualistic position of all 28 Āgamas, clearly distinguishing Śaiva-siddhānta from other Śaiva schools.

all_historical_figures.name: Śrīkaṇṭha
all_historical_figures.role: Master in Sadyojyoti's lineage / Vīra-śaiva philosopher
all_historical_figures.significance: Two figures with the same name are mentioned. One authored Ratna-traya in the Siddhānta tradition. The other wrote a commentary on the Vedānta-sūtras (c. 1122 A.D.) which formed the philosophical basis for Vīra-śaivism.

all_historical_figures.name: Kadamba-guhā-vāsi
all_historical_figures.significance: Headed a Śaiva monastic settlement of the Siddhānta division in Central India, indicating its early presence there.

all_historical_figures.name: Rudra-śambhu
all_historical_figures.significance: Established a sanctuary in Āmardaka (Ujjayinī) and became the royal preceptor to the Kākatiya kings, spreading Siddhānta influence.

all_historical_figures.name: Rājendra I
all_historical_figures.significance: Is reported to have brought Śaiva-siddhānta teachers from North India to the Coḷa country, boosting the tradition's presence in the South.

all_historical_figures.name: Appar (Tiru-Nāvukkarasu)
all_historical_figures.significance: A key figure in the Bhakti movement in Tamil Nadu, his devotional hymns (part of the Tevāram) helped spread Śaivism among the masses.

all_historical_figures.name: Tiru-Jñāna-sam-bandar
all_historical_figures.significance: Along with Appar, he was responsible for the spread of Śaivism in the Pallava and Pāṇḍya territories through his hymns.

all_historical_figures.name: Sundarar
all_historical_figures.significance: One of the three main authors of the Tevāram hymns.

all_historical_figures.name: Tiru-mūlar
all_historical_figures.significance: Author of the Tirumantiram, an important Tamil Śaiva text. Said to have brought the 28 Āgamas to the Tamil country.

all_historical_figures.name: Māṇikka-vācakar
all_historical_figures.significance: Author of the celebrated Tiru-vācakam. The text notes a conflict in his dating.
all_historical_figures.dates: second or third century OR 9th century A.D.

all_historical_figures.name: Nambi-Āṇḍār-Nambi
all_historical_figures.significance: Redacted the devotional songs of the Tamil saints into the twelve books of the Tirumurai.

all_historical_figures.name: Meykaṇḍa-deva
all_historical_figures.significance: Authored the Śiva-jñāna-bodham, a foundational philosophical text of Tamil Śaiva-siddhānta.

all_historical_figures.name: Aruḷ-nandi-Śivācārya
all_historical_figures.significance: Explained and popularized the teachings of Meykaṇḍa-deva.

all_historical_figures.name: Umā-pati-Śivācārya
all_historical_figures.significance: Also explained and popularized the teachings of Meykaṇḍa-deva.

all_historical_figures.name: Basava
all_historical_figures.significance: A pivotal figure in the Vīra-śaiva movement in Karnataka.

all_historical_figures.name: Allama-prabhu
all_historical_figures.significance: Became the first leader of the 'Śūnya-siṁhāsana' (Throne of the Void), an academy of mystics in the Vīra-śaiva movement.

all_historical_figures.name: Sadyojyoti
all_historical_figures.significance: Brought out the dualistic outlook of the Āgamas, especially Rauravāgama, through his gloss (vṛtti). Wrote seven treatises.
all_historical_figures.dates: Mentioned as the teacher of Rājanaka-Ramakantha I (11th c.) and preceded by his own teacher (9th c.).

all_historical_figures.name: Sadyojyoti's teacher
all_historical_figures.significance: Began the list of eighteen masters of Śaiva-siddhānta.

all_historical_figures.name: Rājanaka-Ramakantha I
all_historical_figures.significance: Author of Ratna-traya.

all_historical_figures.name: Bhoja
all_historical_figures.role: King of the Paramāra dynasty of Gujarat, author
all_historical_figures.significance: Wrote Tat-tva-prakāśikā, which became a standard text of Śaiva-siddhānta explaining Śiva through thirty-six categories.

all_historical_figures.name: Srikumāra-deva
all_historical_figures.significance: Attempted to foist a non-dualistic (bhedābheda) interpretation on Bhoja's Tat-tva-prakāśikā with his commentary Tātparya-dīpikā.

all_historical_figures.name: T. Ganapati Sastri
all_historical_figures.significance: Edited Srikumāra-deva's Tātparya-dīpikā (Trivandrum, 1920) and Īśāna-Śiva's Tantra-sāra-paddhati (Trivandrum, 1920).

all_historical_figures.name: Aghora-śiva
all_historical_figures.significance: Wrote an effective rejoinder to Srikumāra-deva, defending the dualistic outlook of Bhoja's work. Presided over the Āmardaka division branch in Chidambaram. Wrote Kriyā-krama-dyotinī.
all_historical_figures.dates: about 1158; also mentioned as 12th century A.D.

all_historical_figures.name: N. Krishna Sastri
all_historical_figures.significance: Edited Aghora-śiva's commentary on Bhoja's work.

all_historical_figures.name: Paramānanda
all_historical_figures.significance: His Śaiva-bhūśaṇa provides a list of eighteen masters of Śaiva-siddhānta.

all_historical_figures.name: Ugra-jyoti
all_historical_figures.significance: First in the list of 18 masters. Teacher of Sadyo-jyoti in one version of the lineage.

all_historical_figures.name: Rāma-kantha
all_historical_figures.significance: Third in the list of 18 masters; disciple of Sadyo-jyoti from Kāśmīra who wrote Sadvṛtti.

all_historical_figures.name: Durvāsa
all_historical_figures.significance: Begins an alternative version of the list of masters, having received instructions from Śiva himself.

all_historical_figures.name: Piṅgala
all_historical_figures.significance: Teacher of Ugra-jyoti in the alternative lineage.

all_historical_figures.name: Śrīkantha
all_historical_figures.significance: Author of Ratna-traya, which expounds the dualistic standpoint.

all_historical_figures.name: Nārāyaṇa-kantha
all_historical_figures.significance: Prepared a gloss on Mṛgendrāgama and a commentary (Bṛhaṭṭīkā) on Sadyojyoti's Tattva-saṁgraha. Quoted as a commentator on upāgamas.

all_historical_figures.name: Soma-śambhu
all_historical_figures.significance: Wrote Krama-kāṇḍa-kramāvali (Soma-śambhu-paddhati), the oldest available Siddhānta work. Ninth in the list of masters.

all_historical_figures.name: Īśāna-Śiva
all_historical_figures.significance: Probable author of the encyclopedic Tantra-sāra-paddhati (Īśāna-śiva-gurudeva-paddhati). Seventeenth in the list of masters.

all_historical_figures.name: The five sages (Agastya, Gautama, Bhāradvāja, Kāśyapa, Kauśika)
all_historical_figures.significance: Obtained initiation from the five heads of Sadāśiva. Their descendants are the ādi-śaivas.

all_historical_figures.name: Atri
all_historical_figures.significance: Named as one of the five sages in an alternative list from Vīrāgama.

all_historical_figures.name: Nandika
all_historical_figures.significance: Named as one of the five sages in a list from Rauravāgama.

all_historical_figures.name: Kuṇḍa and Gola
all_historical_figures.significance: Progenitors of the Upa-śaiva types.

all_historical_figures.name: Kṛṣṇa Śarmā
all_historical_figures.significance: Edited Pratiṣṭhā-lakṣaṇa-sāra-samuccaya.

all_historical_figures.name: Nijaguṇa
all_historical_figures.significance: Cited in Viveka-cintāmaṇi for giving the total number of verses in the Āgama corpus.

all_historical_figures.name: Bhaṭṭa-Nārāyaṇa-kaṇṭha
all_historical_figures.significance: Commented on Mṛgendrāgama, explaining the process of dīkṣā.

all_historical_figures.name: Aghora-śiva
all_historical_figures.significance: Commented on Bhoja-deva's Tattva-prakāśa. His interpretations on the nature of 'pāśa' and Śiva are cited.

all_historical_figures.name: Bhoja-deva
all_historical_figures.significance: Author of Tattva-prakāśa, a foundational text of Śaiva Siddhānta. His definitions of 'pāśa' are discussed.

all_historical_figures.name: Bhaṭṭa-Vāmadeva
all_historical_figures.significance: Author of 'Janma-maraṇa-vicāra', quoted for the definition of 'svatantrya' as 'ānandaśaktiḥ'. Associated with Kashmir Śaivism.

all_historical_figures.name: Kṣemarāja
all_historical_figures.significance: A major figure in Kashmir Śaivism, his commentary on Bhaṭṭa-nārāyaṇa's Stava-cintāmaṇai is cited.

all_historical_figures.name: Bhaṭṭa-nārāyaṇa
all_historical_figures.significance: Author of 'Stava-cintāmaṇai', quoted regarding Śiva's power to undo the snares of māyā.

all_historical_figures.name: Rāma-kaṇṭha
all_historical_figures.significance: Commentator on 'Mataṅga-pārameśvara', quoted on how pure knowledge uproots ignorance when Śiva's energy descends.

all_historical_figures.name: Jayaratha
all_historical_figures.significance: Commentator on Abhinavagupta's 'Tantrāloka', cited for his alternative view of 'mala' as ignorance rather than a substance.

all_historical_figures.name: Ananta
all_historical_figures.significance: Mentioned as the head of the vidyeśvaras, who are responsible for the 'impure' creation. Also listed as one of the eight forms of Śiva in the Īśvara category.

all_historical_figures.name: Śiva
all_historical_figures.significance: The supreme consciousness (akula), communicator of Āgama texts.

all_historical_figures.name: Śakti / Girijā
all_historical_figures.significance: The supreme energy (kula), communicator of Nigama texts, the ultimate object of worship in Śākta-āgama.

all_historical_figures.name: Vāsudeva
all_historical_figures.significance: Mentioned in a quote distinguishing Āgama from Nigama, possibly referring to the Vaiṣṇava tradition's sanction.

all_historical_figures.name: Matsyendra-nātha (Mīna-pā)
all_historical_figures.significance: Regarded by Kāśmīri Kaulas as the first exponent of Kulāgama. Lived around 800 A.D.

all_historical_figures.name: Abhinavagupta
all_historical_figures.significance: Author of Tantrāloka, cited for his description of Kaulas and his mention of 64 Bhairava-tantras.

all_historical_figures.name: Jayaratha
all_historical_figures.significance: Commentator on Tantrāloka, cited regarding Matsyendra-nātha.

all_historical_figures.name: Nārāyaṇa-kaṇṭha
all_historical_figures.significance: Commentator on Mṛgendrāgama, noted the distinction between Śaivas and Śāktas.

all_historical_figures.name: Paraśurāma
all_historical_figures.significance: Author of the Paraśurāma-kalpa-sūtra, a key text of the Śākta tradition.

all_historical_figures.name: Amogha-vajra
all_historical_figures.significance: Translated 77 tantras in China, some of which were Śākta in nature.

all_historical_figures.name: Gauḍapāda
all_historical_figures.significance: Traditionally the guru of Govinda. Wrote several Śākta tantrik works like Śrī-vidyā-ratna-sūtra, crystallizing the Śrī-vidyā school.

all_historical_figures.name: Govinda
all_historical_figures.significance: Student of Gauḍapāda and guru of Śaṃkarācārya. Said to have authored Jayadratha-yāmāla.

all_historical_figures.name: Śaṃkarācārya
all_historical_figures.significance: Major philosopher of Advaita Vedānta, also claimed by Tantric tradition as an adept in Śrī-vidyā who popularized the cult. Works like Saundarya-laharī are ascribed to him. Wrongly credited with writing Prapañca-sāra.

all_historical_figures.name: Padmapāda
all_historical_figures.significance: Wrote Sambandha-dīpikā, a gloss on Prapañca-sāra.

all_historical_figures.name: Lolla-Lakṣmīdhara
all_historical_figures.significance: A key figure in the Śākta renaissance, wrote commentaries on Saundarya-lahari and Subhagodaya.

all_historical_figures.name: Bhāskara-rāya-makhi (Bhāsurānanda-nātha)
all_historical_figures.significance: An eminent authority and a leader of the Śākta purge and renaissance. Wrote a famous gloss on Lalitā-sahasra-nāma (1728) and a commentary on Nityā-ṣoḍaśikārṇava (1733).

all_historical_figures.name: Umānanda-nātha
all_historical_figures.significance: Student of Bhāskara-rāya, brought the definitive text of Samayācāra, Paraśu-rāma-kalpa-sūtra, to prominence with his commentary.

all_historical_figures.name: Manu
all_historical_figures.significance: Cited from his work (op.cit) on the classification of 'mohana' (attraction) as a primary magical deed (mūla-karma).

complete_timeline.event: Reign of Coḷa emperor Rājendra I.
complete_timeline.significance: Facilitated the exchange of Śaiva traditions between North and South India.

complete_timeline.event: Reign of King Bhoja of the Paramāra dynasty
complete_timeline.significance: Period when the influential dualistic text 'Tat-tva-prakāśikā' was composed.

complete_timeline.event: Belūr inscription of Jayasiṁha
complete_timeline.significance: Refers to a 'traipuruṣa' temple built by Akkadevī who followed rituals of five different deities.

complete_timeline.event: Ṣikāripura inscription of Nāga-varma
complete_timeline.significance: An officer builds four separate shrines for Jina, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and Buddha.

complete_timeline.event: Kannaḍa inscription from Karnūl describes the Kālāmukha teacher Sureśvara-paṇḍita-deva.
complete_timeline.significance: Provides details on the identity and spread of the Kālāmukha sect.

complete_timeline.event: Nāgadevayya builds the Nāgeśvara temple and a township for prostitutes at Sūndi.
complete_timeline.significance: Shows the institutionalization of temple prostitution under Śaiva patronage.

complete_timeline.event: Reign of Vikramāditya VI
complete_timeline.significance: A Śaiva king patronizing Buddhist sites and including Viṣṇu imagery in a Śiva temple.

complete_timeline.event: Flourishing period of the Kōḍiya-maṭha at Balligāme.
complete_timeline.significance: Represents the peak of Kālāmukha monastic centers as hubs of education and social welfare.

complete_timeline.event: Reign of Hoysala king Viṣṇuvardhana
complete_timeline.significance: A Jaina king building the famous Vaiṣṇava Keśava temple at Belūr.

complete_timeline.event: Balligāme inscription mentioning 'Hari-Hara-Kamalāsana-Vitarāga-Baud-dhalayangaḷ'
complete_timeline.significance: Refers to shrines for Viṣṇu, Śiva, Brahmā, Jina, and Buddha, calling them 'five streams irrigating the earth'.

complete_timeline.event: Reign of Kalacūri-Bijjaḷa of Kalyāṇa.
complete_timeline.significance: The political context for the rise of Basava and the Vīraśaiva movement.

complete_timeline.event: Kaiḍāļa inscription with syncretic verse
complete_timeline.significance: Pays obeisance to one principle manifesting as Śiva, Brahmā, Buddha, Viṣṇu, and Jina.

complete_timeline.event: Establishment of the 'Śūnya-siṁhāsana' in Kalyāṇa.
complete_timeline.significance: A major event in the Vīra-śaiva movement, creating a center for spiritual discourse and reform.

complete_timeline.event: Period of decline for the Kālāmukha sect.
complete_timeline.significance: Marks a major shift in the religious landscape of Karnataka with the rise of Vīraśaivism.

complete_timeline.event: An inscription describes the multifaceted functions of the Kōḍiya-maṭha.
complete_timeline.significance: Provides a detailed primary source account of the socio-educational role of a Kālāmukha monastery.

complete_timeline.event: Polāļva builds a Hari-Hara shrine
complete_timeline.significance: Construction of a dedicated temple for the syncretic Śiva-Viṣṇu deity.

complete_timeline.event: Reigns of Harihara I and Bukka of Vijayanagara.
complete_timeline.significance: The Kālāmukha sect still held influence, with its teachers serving as royal preceptors (Rājaguru).

complete_timeline.event: Inscription records charity for feeding 'ubhaya-jaṅgamas' (both Nātha-siddha and Kālāmukha ascetics).
complete_timeline.significance: Evidence of the co-existence and fusion of the two sects.

complete_timeline.event: Vidyāśaṅkara shrine at Śṛṅgeri is built in connection with the Kālāmukha teacher Kāśivilāsa-kriyāśakti.
complete_timeline.significance: Shows the continued prestige of Kālāmukha teachers even as the sect's general influence was waning.

complete_timeline.event: Reign of Kṛṣṇadeva-rāya
complete_timeline.significance: A Vaiṣṇava emperor making large grants to Śaiva temples.

complete_timeline.event: Bhāskara-rāya writes his gloss on Lalitā-sahasra-nāma.
complete_timeline.significance: A landmark work in the history of Śrī-vidyā and the Samayācāra tradition.

complete_timeline.event: Bhāskara-rāya writes his commentary on Nityā-ṣoḍaśikārṇava.
complete_timeline.significance: Another major contribution solidifying his authority and the reformed Śākta tradition.

complete_timeline.event: Nānāghāṭ inscription of Nāganikā
complete_timeline.significance: Early inscription mentioning worship of male deities like Indra, Sankarṣaṇa, Vāsudeva.

complete_timeline.event: Creation of a bronze seal with Śiva's image and the name 'Śiva-rakṣita'.
complete_timeline.significance: Early archaeological evidence of iconic representation of Śiva.

complete_timeline.event: Life of Lakulīśa, founder of the Pāśupata sect.
complete_timeline.significance: Pivotal moment in the systematization of Śaivism as a formal philosophical and religious system.

complete_timeline.event: Reign of Aśoka; he allegedly built a Śiva shrine in Kashmir.
complete_timeline.significance: Possible early royal patronage of Śaivism by a non-Śaiva emperor.

complete_timeline.event: Vākāṭaka rulers adopt Śaiva titles.
complete_timeline.significance: Demonstrates the deep integration of Śaivism with royal identity in the Deccan.

complete_timeline.event: Possible lifetime of Māṇikka-vācakar (early date).
complete_timeline.significance: Represents the ancient roots of Tamil Śaiva devotionalism.

complete_timeline.event: Land grant by Kākutstha-Varma
complete_timeline.significance: A Vedic follower patronizing a Jaina ascetic.

complete_timeline.event: Grants by Mṛgeśa-varma
complete_timeline.significance: Royal patronage for Jaina shrines.

complete_timeline.event: Life of Kauṇḍinya, Pāśupata commentator.
complete_timeline.significance: Development of scholastic tradition within the Pāśupata sect.

complete_timeline.event: Ravi-varma builds a Jinālaya
complete_timeline.significance: Construction of a Jain temple by a Kadamba ruler.

complete_timeline.event: Excavation of Viṣṇu-gṛha (Cave 3) at Bādāmi by Maṅgalīśa
complete_timeline.significance: A major Cālukyan rock-cut temple dedicated to the trinity, initiated by a Vaiṣṇava and completed by a Śaiva.

complete_timeline.event: Reign of Pallava monarch Mahendra-varma I.
complete_timeline.significance: Period of the flourishing of the Bhakti movement led by saints like Appar.

complete_timeline.event: Reign of Maṅgalīśa; inscriptions show patronage to Śaiva temples.
complete_timeline.significance: Early evidence of the Lākula cult's popularity in Karnataka.

complete_timeline.event: Kālāmukhas enter Karnataka from Śrīśaila.
complete_timeline.significance: Beginning of the sect's expansion and eventual dominance in the South.

complete_timeline.event: Inscription records a village grant to Kapāleśvara temple and mentions Kālāmukha ascetics.
complete_timeline.significance: Early evidence of Kālāmukhas administering temples.

complete_timeline.event: Reign of Vijayāditya and construction of Vijayeśvara temple
complete_timeline.significance: Building of a 'trai-puruśa' temple in Bādāmi.

complete_timeline.event: Career of Amogha-vajra in China, translating Tantric texts.
complete_timeline.significance: Shows the transmission and existence of Śākta-related tantras by the mid-8th century.

complete_timeline.event: First known inscriptional mention of temple-prostitutes (devadāsīs).
complete_timeline.significance: Marks the beginning of the recorded history of a controversial but long-standing temple practice.

complete_timeline.event: Activity of Nayanmar saints Appar, Tiru-Jñāna-sam-bandar, and Sundarar.
complete_timeline.significance: Composition of the Tevāram hymns and widespread popularization of Śaivism in the Tamil region.

complete_timeline.event: A copy of Parameśvari-tantra is made.
complete_timeline.significance: Provides manuscript evidence for the existence of specific tantras.

complete_timeline.event: Inscription adoring all three deities of the trinity
complete_timeline.significance: Shows continued worship of Brahmā until at least the 9th century.

complete_timeline.event: A copy of Kiraṇa-tantra (a Śākta text, not the Śaiva one) is made.
complete_timeline.significance: Further manuscript evidence for early Śākta texts.

complete_timeline.event: Kāḍiyūr inscription mentioning 'catus-samaya-devatā-nilaya'
complete_timeline.significance: Evidence of temples housing deities of four different sects together.

complete_timeline.event: A vihāra (Buddhist monastery) was built on Kadari hill, Mangalore.
complete_timeline.significance: Indicates the presence of multiple religious traditions in a region later known for the fusion of Buddhism and Śaivism.

complete_timeline.event: Advent of the Nātha-siddha cult in Karnataka.
complete_timeline.significance: Led to the fusion of Nātha-siddha and Kālāmukha ideologies, particularly in coastal regions.

complete_timeline.event: Lifetime of Sadyojyoti.
complete_timeline.significance: Systematization of the Śaiva-siddhānta school and the first use of the term 'Siddhānta'.

complete_timeline.event: Life of Sadyojyoti's teacher
complete_timeline.significance: Marks the beginning of the lineage of 18 Śaiva-siddhānta masters listed by Paramānanda.

complete_timeline.event: Creation of the earliest known mukha-linga at Khoh.
complete_timeline.significance: Development in Śaiva iconography, combining aniconic and iconic forms.

complete_timeline.event: Rule of Sātavāhana kings
complete_timeline.significance: Period when Śaiva rulers built Buddhist shrines, showing religious plurality.

complete_timeline.event: Activity of Abhinava-gupta.
complete_timeline.significance: The peak of Kāśmīr Śaivism's philosophical development.

complete_timeline.event: Activity of Aghora-śiva
complete_timeline.significance: A major defense of the dualistic interpretation of Śaiva-siddhānta was mounted, solidifying its position in the Coḷa country.

complete_timeline.event: Patañjali's Mahābhāṣya mentions 'Śiva-bhāgavatas' and the sale of icons by Mauryas.
complete_timeline.significance: Explicit reference to an organized group of Śiva devotees and the commercialization of religious icons.

complete_timeline.event: Rule of Ālupa rulers of Tuḷunāḍu
complete_timeline.significance: Rulers, mainly Śaiva, built shrines for Viṣṇu and Śakti and encouraged other cults.

complete_timeline.event: Karhaḍ inscription of Kṛṣṇa III records a grant to a Śaiva ascetic.
complete_timeline.significance: Example of Rāṣṭrakūṭa royal patronage for the Śaiva sect.

complete_timeline.event: Decline of 'trai-puruśa' temples
complete_timeline.significance: Marks the wane of Brahmā worship and a shift towards more distinct Śaiva/Vaiṣṇava identities.

complete_timeline.event: Activity of Srikumāra-deva
complete_timeline.significance: An attempt was made to interpret Bhoja's dualistic work from a non-dualistic (bhedābheda) perspective.

complete_timeline.event: Formation of the Gupta Empire; crystallization of Śaiva religion.
complete_timeline.significance: Śaivism becomes a more established and formally recognized religion, with royal patronage.

complete_timeline.event: Pāṇini's work demonstrates knowledge of Śiva's alternate names.
complete_timeline.significance: Early literary evidence for the worship of the god who would be known as Śiva.

complete_timeline.event: Emergence of Āgamas
complete_timeline.date: around the seventh and eighth centuries
complete_timeline.significance: Codification of sectarian worship, leading to the crystallization of distinct cults.

complete_timeline.event: Kālāmukhas continue to be mentioned in inscriptions.
complete_timeline.significance: Indicates the sect's lingering presence long after its peak.

complete_timeline.event: Inscription with syncretic verse praising Buddha, Jina, Viṣṇu, Śiva etc.
complete_timeline.significance: Early inscriptional evidence for the concept of a single Godhead with multiple forms.

complete_timeline.event: Śrīkaṇṭha writes his commentary on the Vedānta-sūtras.
complete_timeline.significance: Provided the philosophical foundation for the emerging Vīra-śaivism sect.

complete_timeline.event: Activity of Aghora-śiva.
complete_timeline.significance: A key moment in the defense and definition of the dualistic Śaiva-siddhānta position.

complete_timeline.event: Activity of Basava and other Vīra-śaiva saints.
complete_timeline.significance: The Vīra-śaiva movement gains considerable force as a movement for religious and social reform.

complete_timeline.event: Lifetime of Meykaṇḍa-deva.
complete_timeline.significance: Composition of Śiva-jñāna-bodham, a seminal text for Tamil Śaiva-siddhānta philosophy.

complete_timeline.event: Lolla-Lakṣmīdhara's period of activity.
complete_timeline.significance: Beginning of the Śākta renaissance, focusing on refined interpretations.

complete_timeline.event: Gauḍapāda writes Śākta tantrik works, crystallizing the Śrī-vidyā school.
complete_timeline.significance: An early documented formation of a key Śākta school of thought.

complete_timeline.event: Lifetime of Tiru-mūlar.
complete_timeline.significance: Authoring of Tirumantiram and the claimed transmission of Āgamic knowledge to the South.

complete_timeline.event: Inscription refers to a Kālāmukha maṭha at Nandi.
complete_timeline.significance: Shows the establishment of Kālāmukha monastic centers in Karnataka.

complete_timeline.event: Leadership of Kadamba-guhā-vāsi in a Central Indian Siddhānta monastery.
complete_timeline.significance: Provides inscriptional evidence for the organized presence of Śaiva-siddhānta in Central India.

complete_timeline.event: Life of Matsyendranātha, exponent of Kulāgama.
complete_timeline.significance: Marks the influence of Nātha-siddha saints on the development of Śākta-tantra.

complete_timeline.event: Vasugupta popularizes the Śiva-sūtra.
complete_timeline.significance: Marks the historical origin of Kāśmīr Śaivism as a distinct non-dualistic school.

complete_timeline.event: Somānanda writes Śiva-dṛṣṭi.
complete_timeline.significance: Establishes the Pratyabhijñā school of Kāśmīr Śaivism.

complete_timeline.event: Activity of Rājanaka-Ramakantha I and Soma-śambhu
complete_timeline.significance: A period of significant literary production in the dualistic Śaiva-siddhānta school.

all_geographic_locations.context: The subject of the entire chapter, described as a land of religious tolerance.
all_geographic_locations.significance: The macro-location for all discussed historical and religious developments.

all_geographic_locations.context: Used as an illustrative example of religious harmony and royal patronage.
all_geographic_locations.significance: Many of the key dynasties and inscriptions cited (Sātavāhana, Kadamba, Cālukya, Hoysala) are from this region.

all_geographic_locations.context: Site of the Tārā-Bhagavatī temple (Buddhist) built by Sātavāhanas. Also site of shrines for five faiths mentioned in a 1129 inscription.
all_geographic_locations.significance: A key site demonstrating long-term religious pluralism and patronage.

all_geographic_locations.context: Site of stūpas (Buddhist monuments) built by Sātavāhanas.
all_geographic_locations.significance: Example of Śaiva rulers supporting Buddhism.

all_geographic_locations.context: Capital of the Kadambas, described as a great centre of Buddhism.
all_geographic_locations.significance: Shows a capital city fostering multiple religions under its ruling dynasty.

all_geographic_locations.context: In Belgaum district, where Ravi-varma built a Jinālaya (Jain temple).
all_geographic_locations.significance: Specific site of Kadamba patronage to Jainism.

all_geographic_locations.context: Location of Palasikā.
all_geographic_locations.significance: Geographic context for Kadamba activity.

all_geographic_locations.context: Capital of the Gaṅgas, who were Jainas but built many temples to Śiva and Viṣṇu.
all_geographic_locations.significance: Example of Jaina rulers patronizing Hindu deities.

all_geographic_locations.context: Site of the famous rock-cut Viṣṇu-gṛha (Cave 3) and the Vijayeśvara temple, both housing the trinity.
all_geographic_locations.significance: A major centre for the Cālukyas and a prime example of 'traipuruṣa' worship.

all_geographic_locations.context: Region ruled by the Ālupas. Also location of later Hari-Hara shrines.
all_geographic_locations.significance: Region showing a mix of Śaiva, Jaina, Vaiṣṇava, and Śakti worship.

all_geographic_locations.context: Site of the Keśava temple built by Viṣṇuvardhana. Also location of a Hoysala period inscription.
all_geographic_locations.significance: A major Hoysala center and site of significant Vaiṣṇava architecture and syncretic inscriptions.

all_geographic_locations.context: Capital of a later Cālukyan dynasty.
all_geographic_locations.significance: Identifies the dynasty of Vikramāditya VI.

all_geographic_locations.context: Site of a Buddhist vihāra endowed by Vikramāditya VI.
all_geographic_locations.significance: Example of a Śaiva king's patronage to Buddhism.

all_geographic_locations.context: Site of a Śiva temple built by Vikramāditya VI containing impressive Viṣṇu sculptures.
all_geographic_locations.significance: Demonstrates syncretism within a single temple structure.

all_geographic_locations.context: Śiva temple that received endowments from the Vaiṣṇava king Kṛṣṇadeva-rāya.
all_geographic_locations.significance: Example of Vijayanagara cross-sectarian patronage.

all_geographic_locations.context: Śiva temple that received endowments from the Vaiṣṇava king Kṛṣṇadeva-rāya.
all_geographic_locations.significance: Example of Vijayanagara cross-sectarian patronage.

all_geographic_locations.context: In Tumkur district, site of an inscription from 1151 A.D. with a syncretic verse.
all_geographic_locations.significance: Source of primary inscriptional evidence for religious harmony.

all_geographic_locations.context: Location of Kaiḍāļa.
all_geographic_locations.significance: Geographic context for the 1151 A.D. inscription.

all_geographic_locations.context: Location of the praśasti of Kokkalla-māharāja.
all_geographic_locations.significance: Source of an inscription praising an all-comprehensive God.

all_geographic_locations.context: In Karnataka, site of a 'catus-samaya-devatā-nilaya' (shrine for deities of four sects) mentioned in a 929 A.D. inscription.
all_geographic_locations.significance: Direct evidence of multi-faith temple complexes.

all_geographic_locations.context: A northern region site with a shrine for Brahmā.
all_geographic_locations.significance: One of the few remaining centers of Brahmā worship.

all_geographic_locations.context: Site of a 1048 A.D. inscription mentioning the construction of four shrines.
all_geographic_locations.significance: Evidence of parallel patronage to four different faiths.

all_geographic_locations.context: Site of the Konti-guḍi, Huccap-payya-maṭha, and Tryambakeśvara temple complex, showing trinity worship.
all_geographic_locations.significance: An important Cālukyan center with numerous temples showing sectarian evolution.

all_geographic_locations.context: Site of the Trikūṭeśvara temple with three lingas for Brahmā, Śiva, and Viṣṇu.
all_geographic_locations.significance: A prime example of a 'tri-kūṭācala' temple dedicated to the trinity.

all_geographic_locations.context: Site of the Banasaṅkari temple, dedicated to all three deities of the trinity.
all_geographic_locations.significance: Another example of a trinity temple.

all_geographic_locations.context: Location of an 11th-century inscription speaking of a joint Śiva-Viṣṇu temple.
all_geographic_locations.significance: Shows that the trend of joint worship was not confined to South India.

all_geographic_locations.context: Site of a shrine to the composite deity Hari-Hara, built in 1223.
all_geographic_locations.significance: An important center for the syncretic Hari-Hara cult.

all_geographic_locations.context: In Tuḷunāḍu, site of a 13th-century Hari-Hara shrine.
all_geographic_locations.significance: Another center for the Hari-Hara cult.

all_geographic_locations.context: Other sites in Tuḷunāḍu with shrines to the composite Hari-Hara deity.
all_geographic_locations.significance: Shows the popularity of the Hari-Hara cult in this specific region.

all_geographic_locations.context: Region where the bulk of the Āgamas were likely composed during the Pallava and early Cola periods.
all_geographic_locations.significance: The heartland for the development of the scriptural basis for sectarian Śaivism and Vaiṣṇavism.

all_geographic_locations.context: Site of Nāganikā's inscription.
all_geographic_locations.significance: Source of early epigraphic evidence on Sātavāhana religious practices.

all_geographic_locations.context: Mentioned as a site with early evidence for the worship of Śiva.
all_geographic_locations.significance: Suggests prehistoric roots for Śiva worship.

all_geographic_locations.context: Site of Aśoka's alleged shrine (Aśokeśvara); a major center for the development of Śaiva theology and metaphysics.
all_geographic_locations.significance: A key region for the intellectual and sectarian development of Śaivism.

all_geographic_locations.context: Site where John Marśal found a 1st century B.C. bronze seal depicting Śiva.
all_geographic_locations.significance: Provides early archaeological evidence for the iconic representation of Śiva.

all_geographic_locations.context: Site where the earliest mukha-linga was found.
all_geographic_locations.significance: Important for the history of Śaiva iconography.

all_geographic_locations.context: Proposed as the region where Śaivism was first organized as a sect, before spreading.
all_geographic_locations.significance: The author's hypothesized heartland for organized Śaivism.

all_geographic_locations.context: A region where Śaivism spread and flourished, particularly through the Kālāmukha sect.
all_geographic_locations.significance: Became a major center of Śaivism, developing unique regional forms like Vīra-Śaivism.

all_geographic_locations.context: Listed as an ancient and important center of Śiva worship.
all_geographic_locations.significance: One of the most sacred and enduring centers of Śaivism.

all_geographic_locations.context: An ancient Śaiva center; the region where Lakulīśa appeared.
all_geographic_locations.significance: Crucial location for the origin of the Pāśupata sect.

all_geographic_locations.context: Identified as the specific birthplace of Lakulīśa.
all_geographic_locations.significance: The origin point of the historical founder of the Pāśupata sect.

all_geographic_locations.context: The starting point from which the Kālāmukhas entered the Telugu country and Karnataka.

complete_terminology_index.translation: (Sanskrit Chhaya: īpaśupate roṣāruṇapratimāsaṁkrāntagaurīmukhacandram। gṛhītārdhapaṅkajamiva sandhyāsalilāñjaliṁ namatā ||) Bow down to the handful of evening twilight water of Paśupati, which is like a half-plucked lotus, with the moon of Gaurī's face reflected in it, reddened by his anger.
complete_terminology_index.context: Prakrit verse from Hāla's Gāthā-saptaśatī invoking Śiva and Gauri.

complete_terminology_index.translation: The religion or system of beliefs and practices centered on the god Śiva.
complete_terminology_index.context: The main subject of the chapter.
An early name for Rudra/Śiva known to Pāṇini.

An early name for Rudra/Śiva known to Pāṇini.
Used by Patañjali to refer to icons of Śiva, Skanda, and Viśākhā.

complete_terminology_index.term: अपण्य इत्युच्यते तत्रेदं न सिध्यति । शिवं स्कन्दो विशाख इति । किं कारणं? मौर्यैर्हिरण्यार्थिभिरर्चाः प्रकल्पिताः ॥
complete_terminology_index.transliteration: apaṇya ityucyate tatredaṁ na sidhyati । śivaṁ skando viśākha iti । kiṁ kāraṇaṁ? mauryairhiraṇyārthibhirarcāḥ prakalpitāḥ ॥
complete_terminology_index.translation: It is said 'not for sale', but this does not apply here to (the icons of) Śiva, Skanda, and Viśākha. What is the reason? Because the icons were set up by the gold-seeking Mauryas.
complete_terminology_index.context: Quoted from Patañjali's Mahābhāṣya regarding the sale of religious icons.
The author notes worship in this form had likely not come into vogue when Patañjali wrote.

complete_terminology_index.translation: A linga with a face (or faces) of Śiva carved on it.
complete_terminology_index.context: The earliest example found at Khoh dates to the early Gupta period.
A name for Śiva, worshipped by Mihira-gula.
The oldest sect of Śaivism, founded by Lakulīśa.

complete_terminology_index.translation: secret, secret and beyond, exceeding secret, sacred, enduring
complete_terminology_index.context: Classifications for traditional Śaiva centers.
The Mahābhārata refers to Pāśupata as one of the 'Jñānas'.
The Mahābhārata refers to Pāśupata as one of the 'matas'.
The textual foundation upon which the Pāśupata sect and its offshoots rely.
The three philosophies taught by Durvāsas's disciples in Kāśmir Śaivism.
A description of Lakulīśa.
Monastic settlements built by the Kālāmukhas, which became centers of learning and welfare.
The Sanskrit root for the Kannaḍa term 'parṣhe', referring to territorial jurisdictions of the Kālāmukhas.
A title claimed by the Noḷamba kings, showing their patronage.
A term the Lākula teachers used for themselves, indicating their Vedic orientation.

complete_terminology_index.translation: Place of the god (deva) and place of residence (sthāna)
complete_terminology_index.context: An expression for a temple that became popular under Kālāmukha influence, reflecting its dual function.
Titles for the Kālāmukha teachers who administered temples and their associated schools.
Vāmaśakti-dēva was the rājaguru of Keśimayya; Kāśivilāsa-kriyāśakti was the rājaguru of Harihara I and Bukka.
The prescribed observances of a Pāśupata devotee.
A six-fold observance for Pāśupata devotees, including music and dance.

complete_terminology_index.context: The six aspects of the Pāśupata niyama.
Term for temple prostitutes, a feature suggested to be part of Kālāmukha-administered temples.
The individual soul, seen as an effect of the divine cause.
A term for the individual soul, signifying its state of bondage and dependence.
God (Śiva), the ultimate cause of everything.
A term for God (Śiva) as the lord of all individual souls (paśu).
The forces that bind the soul, consisting of mala, māyā, and karma.
The discipline of mind and meditation to achieve spiritual goals.
Worldly conduct based on virtue, conducive to attaining the values of life.
The final cessation of sorrow, or liberation, caused by bondage.
The grace of Śiva, considered the sole cause of liberation in the Pāśupata and Siddhānta schools.
The act of surrendering oneself to God to obtain liberation.
The path of devotion, central to schools like Śaiva-siddhānta.
The philosophical outlook that God, soul, and world are eternally distinct realities.
The philosophical outlook that reality is ultimately one, and the soul is identical to God.
A philosophical position that attempts to reconcile dualistic and non-dualistic views.
Another name for Kāśmir Śaivism, referring to the triad of paśu, pati, and pāśa.
The primary bond (pāśa) that causes ignorance and hides the soul's true nature.
The bond (pāśa) that creates the various planes of existence and experience.
The bond (pāśa) of good and bad actions that results in phenomenal experiences.
The path of wisdom, central to Kāśmir Śaivism.
The core concept of a school of Kāśmir Śaivism, referring to the recognition of the self's divine nature.
The ultimate goal of spiritual practice.
The true, essential nature of the self, which in non-dualism is identical to Śiva.
The name for the codified dualistic Āgama tradition.
The form of Śaivism prevalent in Karnataka, also known as Lingayatism.
A key doctrine in Vīra-śaivism describing the six planes of spiritual experience.
A characteristic doctrine of Vīra-śaivism.
The mystic and direct experience of the divine presence, a key concept in Vīra-śaivism.
The name of the philosophical and religious system being discussed.

complete_terminology_index.translation: That which has come down; traditional doctrine, sacred text.
complete_terminology_index.context: The foundational scriptures of Śaiva-siddhānta.
Sadyojyoti wrote a 'vṛtti' on the Rauravāgama.
The form of most of Sadyojyoti's treatises.
The non-dualistic interpretation foisted by Srikumāra-deva on Bhoja's work.
A manual of instructions for the practice of Siddhānta compiled by each of the 18 masters.
A term for the eighteen masters of Śaiva-siddhānta.
Śiva becomes 'sakala' (assumes form) in order to create.
The inherent energy in Śiva from which creation begins.
The primordial sound that issues from pāra-śakti.
The primeval nucleus that comes from nāda and becomes Sadāśiva.
The five aspects of creation: sṛṣṭi (emanation), sthiti (preservation), saṁhāra (dissolution), tirobhāva (concealment), and anugraha (grace).
Sages and their lineages initiated from the five faces of Śiva.

complete_terminology_index.translation: A person illicitly born of a brahmin in a woman who has her husband alive.
complete_terminology_index.context: A type of Upa-śaiva.

complete_terminology_index.translation: A person illicitly born of a brahmin in a woman who is a widow.
complete_terminology_index.context: A type of Upa-śaiva.
The Siddhānta class of āgama texts, considered superior as they proceed from the upper face of Śiva.
Subsidiary or affiliated texts of the main 28 Āgamas.
The four divisions of an Āgama text: Jñāna, Kriyā, Caryā, Yoga.
The central, indispensable ritual for becoming a Śaiva-siddhāntin.
Burdens and hindrances on the self that are removed by dīkṣā.
The phenomenon of divine energy descending upon the aspirant through the preceptor during dīkṣā.
The four spiritual paths followed by initiates: Dāsa, Putra, Saha, and San-mārga.
The first stage of emancipation, achieved by the 'samayī'.
The second stage of emancipation, achieved by the 'mantra-vṛtti'.
The third stage of emancipation, where one assumes the form of God.
The final stage of emancipation (mokṣa), union with Śiva, achieved by the 'deśika'.
Types of initiation based on the aspirant's capacity to follow the prescribed conduct.
The hereditary priest class, descended from the five sages initiated by Śiva.

complete_terminology_index.translation: For one's own sake / for the sake of others.
complete_terminology_index.context: Private worship vs. public worship, the latter being the exclusive domain of ādi-śaivas.
The five signs worn by all initiated Śaivas: rudrākṣa, upavīta, uttarīya, bhasma, and kaupīna.
The central rite in Śaiva-siddhānta through which a practitioner receives divine grace and is set on the path to liberation.
Contrasted with dīkṣā; knowledge alone is not sufficient for final release.
The immediate purpose of dīkṣā, which involves purifying the six paths of reality.
The six-fold map of reality, comprising mantras, words, letters, worlds, tattvas, and kalās.
The 36 fundamental categories that constitute all of reality, from the gross elements to the supreme Śiva.
Used in multiple senses: one of the pañca-kañcuka (limited power of action), the five cosmic aspects (Nivṛtti, etc.), and the aspects of Śiva's manifestation (niṣkala, sakala).
The first category of the fundamental triad; the Godhead, Śiva.
The second category of the triad; the individual soul bound by impurities.
The third category of the triad; the phenomenon of bondage, comprising mala, karma, and māyā.
The primordial, innate impurity that clouds the soul's consciousness and limits its powers, causing a sense of imperfection.
The bond consisting of the accumulated potencies of past actions, which determines future experiences.
The material cause of the 'impure' universe and the bond that provides the soul with a body and world for its experience.
One of Śiva's five functions; the power that conceals the soul's true nature, enabling it to experience the world.
One of Śiva's five functions; the liberating power that reveals the soul's true nature and grants release.
The highest, transcendent, and formless aspect of Śiva.
The fully manifest, formed aspect of Śiva (as Maheśa). Also refers to the class of souls bound by all three pāśas.
The intermediate aspect of Śiva (as Sadāśiva) which is both with and without form.
A concept peculiar to Śaiva-siddhānta describing the five modes of reality in the sakala-niṣkala phase, representing the integration of tattva and mūrti.
The title of the chapter; the body of sacred texts for the Śākta tradition.
The tradition from which Śākta-āgama is said to have grown.
Texts communicated by Śiva to Śakti or devotees.
Texts revealed by Śakti to Śiva or devotees.
A term often used for Śākta texts, though some Śaiva texts are also called tantras.
A cult, originally Śaiva, now primarily Śākta, focused on the worship of Śakti as Kula.
Represents Śakti in Kaula texts.
Represents Śiva in Kaula texts.
A seven-fold hierarchy of spiritual practices, from vedācāra to kaulācāra.
A private conduct involving the five 'principles' (pañca-tattva).
Three progressive spiritual dispositions: paśu (animal), vīra (heroic), and divya (divine).
The essential ritual for spiritual practice and liberation, given by a guru.
The dormant divine energy at the base of the spine, whose awakening is a central goal.
Psychic energy centers in the subtle body.
A cosmogram (yantra) used in Śrī-vidyā worship, representing the union of Śiva and Śakti.
A sacred formula, considered the sound-form of a deity.
Seed-syllables (bījākṣaras) that are the potent core of mantras.
A ritual of repeated mantra recitation to make the mantra effective.
The traditional schools of Śākta-āgama, typically four or five, associated with cardinal directions.
Five ritual articles used in Vāmācāra: madya (wine), māṃsa (meat), matsya (fish), mudrā (gesture/grain), and maithuna (copulation).
Six magical/occult procedures (paralysing, deluding, killing, etc.) considered tāmasika in nature.
A refined, internalized form of Śākta worship, contrasted with the external rituals of Kaulācāra.
